title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 How Can Teachers Find Clarity in a Sea of Confusing Data?
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Education researcher David Griffith identifies the 'chaotic information environment' as the primary barrier to evidence-based teaching -- older teachers, curricula, and online articles all telling teachers different things. Natalie Wexler introduces The Evidence Checker, an AI tool developed by University of Toronto researchers Nidhi Sachdeva and Jim Hewitt, designed to help teachers navigate contradictory research. Unlike pasting questions directly into a general AI chatbot, The Evidence Checker uses a carefully engineered prompt that instructs the model to behave as an educational research assistant -- critical, accurate, and free of jargon. The tool walks through six structured steps, culminating in a 'What should a reasonable evidence-informed teacher conclude?' section and suggested follow-up questions. Wexler tests it on the knowledge-versus-comprehension-skills debate and finds it provides a genuinely useful, if imperfect, starting point for evidence-informed decision-making. She argues AI used by teachers -- rather than students -- holds real promise for cutting through the noise of an overcrowded information landscape.
points: * Nearly a third of early elementary teachers still use reading methods that conflict with well-established evidence, according to a recent report by David Griffith -- a symptom of the 'chaotic information environment' teachers navigate daily. * The Evidence Checker uses a structured AI prompt from University of Toronto researchers that instructs the model to act as an educational research assistant, avoiding the role of 'motivational speaker, advocate, consultant, or influencer.' * The tool follows six steps, from summarizing the overall state of evidence through to a 'What should a reasonable evidence-informed teacher conclude?' section -- making research findings actionable without distorting them. * When Wexler tested it on the comprehension-skills-vs-knowledge-building debate, the AI correctly identified the false either/or framing while still providing a useful directional answer pointing toward integrated instruction. * AI used by teachers -- rather than students -- can be a powerful force for bringing research clarity into practice, but the tool's quality depends entirely on how well its underlying prompt is constructed.
quotes: An older teacher tells you one thing. Your curriculum tells you something else. You read an article online written by some think tank and it tells you a third thing. Teachers want to do the right thing, [but there's a] lack of clarity... about points that really should be clear. -- David Griffith
The Evidence Checker provides, essentially, a well-designed prompt that tells the model in no uncertain terms what it is supposed to do.
What works best is to put a particular topic or text in the foreground and bring in whatever skills or strategies can best help students understand it. -- Natalie Wexler
This sounds like a great template for prompting an AI model on almost any topic, education-related or not.
AI can be hugely helpful -- especially when used by teachers rather than students. -- Natalie Wexler
